analysis.one_liner: Requires natural gas companies to refund overcharges, with interest, to consumers.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a committee vote or floor vote in the 102nd Congress; it died after one hearing.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would change federal natural gas law so that when regulators find a gas company overcharged its customers, the company must refund the extra money to the people who paid it, with interest. It would also set a deadline window for when those refunds must start, shift the burden of proof onto the gas company to show its rates are fair, and require companies to refile their base rates every three years. It was introduced by Senator Howard Metzenbaum, sent to the Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee, got one subcommittee hearing, and never advanced.
analysis.who_benefits: Customers of federally regulated natural gas companies who are found to have been overcharged. Under the bill, the regulator could order the company to pay back the unjustified portion of its rates directly to those customers, with interest, and companies would have to prove rate increases are justified rather than consumers proving they are not [S3]. It also would speed up decisions on rate complaints, with a required refund start date no earlier than 60 days after a complaint and no later than 210 days after filing [S3].
analysis.who_benefits_short: Natural gas customers who are overcharged

how_it_helps.text: Requires gas companies to refund, with interest, any portion of their rates the regulator finds not justified, paid to the people who actually paid the charges [S3].
Puts the burden of proof on the natural gas company to show a proposed rate change is just and reasonable, instead of leaving it to consumers or the regulator to prove otherwise [S3].

Sets a bounded refund window for complaint cases: the refund effective date cannot start earlier than 60 days after the complaint is filed or later than 150 days after that 60-day period, ending the practice of letting disputes drag on while customers keep paying higher rates [S3].
Requires companies to refile base tariff rates at least every 36 months, giving regulators a regular chance to reexamine rates rather than letting old rates persist [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Federally regulated natural gas companies, which would have to pay refunds plus interest when rates are found unjustified, cover the cost of more frequent rate filings, and carry the burden of proving their rates are fair. To the extent refunds or compliance raise their costs, some of that could show up in future approved rates [S3].
analysis.who_pays_short: Natural gas pipeline and utility companies

drawbacks.text: The bill itself directs a FERC study of its effects on the cost of capital paid by natural gas companies and on how long rate cases take, an acknowledgment that mandatory refunds and proof burdens could raise companies' financing costs and lengthen or complicate proceedings [S3].

Shifting the burden of proof to companies and mandating refunds with interest could make companies more cautious about filing needed rate changes, which supporters of the old system argued could complicate rate setting; the bill's own study provision covers these concerns [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill offered a direct consumer protection: money that regulators found was unjustly collected would go back to the customers who paid it, with interest, instead of staying with the company. The main costs fall on the gas companies and could indirectly affect future rates, and the bill acknowledged this by ordering a study of the effects. It was a targeted fix rather than a sweeping overhaul, but the consumer benefit was clear and the design addressed the main industry objection with a study provision.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee, got one subcommittee hearing in June 1991, and never came up for a committee or floor vote before the 102nd Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Metzenbaum introduced the bill on April 25, 1991, with no cosponsors [S4].
The Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Energy and Natural Resources, which sent it to the Subcommittee on Energy Regulation [S5].
The committee requested comments from the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission, the Department of Energy, and the Office of Management and Budget [S5].
The subcommittee held a hearing on June 19, 1991 (S.Hrg. 102-161), but the full committee never acted and the bill never reached the Senate floor [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Natural gas companies are better off because the bill died: they never had to refund overcharges with interest, carry the burden of proving their rates are fair, or refile base rates every three years.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Natural gas companies that kept overcharges

for.name: Sen. Howard Metzenbaum
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and pursued it through the Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee process.

for.name: Senate Subcommittee on Energy Regulation
for.role: Subcommittee of the Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee
for.what_they_did: Held a hearing on the bill on June 19, 1991 (S.Hrg. 102-161), its only public airing.

against.name: Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee
against.role: Committee of referral (chaired by Sen. J. Bennett Johnston, D-LA)
against.what_they_did: Never reported the bill out of committee or scheduled a markup after the June 1991 hearing, leaving it to die at the end of the 102nd Congress.

sides.party_line_note: The bill had a single Democratic sponsor and no cosponsors in either party, so no party-level pattern of support or opposition appears in the record.

industries.industry: Federally regulated natural gas pipeline and utility companies
industries.note: The bill would have required these companies to refund unjustified charges to customers with interest, prove their own rates are fair, and refile base rates every 36 months. The bill's death meant no mandatory consumer refunds under the Natural Gas Act.

industries.industry: FERC-regulated rate proceedings and industry legal practices
industries.note: The bill would have speeded up complaint hearings and given them priority, changing the pace of rate cases for companies and regulators alike. The bill ordered a study of effects on companies' cost of capital and case timelines, acknowledging the uncertainty.
